Liam / Nina —

Thanks — attached is a short spreadsheet that models three baseline choices (14-day median, 30-day avg, and your supplied point estimate). I modeled burst scenarios at +50%, +100%, and +300% and applied two different protection approaches we can propose in Exhibit B:

- Option A: Banded soft caps with a 14-day rolling true-up and crediting mechanics. Surcharges only kick in after sustained bursts beyond a band (example math in sheet).
- Option B: Immediate model-variant fallback (automated routing to a compatible lower-cost variant) for short bursts, combined with monthly reconciliation for larger sustained overages.

High-level recommendation: For pilots with unpredictable spikes we prefer Option B operationally (keeps SLAs stable and avoids one-off bill shocks) but we can draft language for either.

Kimberly — appreciate any contract-level guidance on the redline points.

Team —

I reviewed MedSync’s PDF redline and Marissa’s scenarios. A few legal suggestions to balance bill predictability with commercial protection:

1) Replace any absolute "hard ceiling" language with a two-tier construct: (i) a "soft band" that triggers operational mitigations (model variant fallback and throttling policy), and (ii) a "reconciliation bucket" computed monthly with a clear formula for credits/surcharges.

2) For burst protection, define a "sustained burst" as >150% of baseline for 3+ consecutive days. Shorter spikes (1–2 days) should be handled operationally via routing to lower-cost variants — not billed as overage. This keeps the pilot safe from single-day anomalies.

3) Avoid predefined daily per-token ceilings tied to calendar days; instead use rolling-window exposure to prevent gaming and to match how traffic behaves.

4) Add an explicit fallback in the SOW that Redwood will provide an example calc for a 30/60/90-day lookback on request (we can automate later).

I’ve attached a marked-up Exhibit B with suggested language. The key negotiation points for commercial are: the threshold for "sustained burst," the duration for reconciliation, and whether the customer wants a hard cap in exchange for lower rates (we can offer an optional capped plan with higher unit price as an opt-in).

If MedSync wants a hard cap we need upfront calibration (longer notice, larger committed capacity) — that’s fair. Otherwise I recommend the banded soft-cap + routing + monthly reconciliation.

-Kim
Senior Counsel, Contracts
Redwood Inference

Thanks for the CSV — attached is a brief follow-up (in the same workbook I shared earlier) that shows:

- Worst-case math for the month under Option B (routing + monthly reconciliation) assuming three separate 3-day sustained bursts at +200% each: incremental invoice = $18,600 on pilot baseline;
- Worst-case math under a hard-cap plan (with a 30% uplift to unit price) using the same burst profile: incremental invoice = $12,100 but notice you pay higher per-unit even in baseline days; detailed table is in tab "cap_vs_softcap".

Practical recommendation: for pilot velocity we usually advise the soft-cap + routing approach — it preserves application latency and avoids surprise invoices on single-day spikes. If MedSync needs absolute budget certainty, the capped plan is available as an opt-in with a 25–35% uplift depending on committed volume (I’ve asked Karthik to add two commit-level rows for your review).
